prompt.context: Your client is an entrepreneur looking to invest in a new sports bar. He needs to determine how profitable the business will be and convince his primary investor — his father — that it will be a viable business.
prompt.question: What factors would you consider and investigate to determine profitability and make a recommendation to the investor?

clarifying_info.q: What does the average customer spend on food per visit?
What does the average customer spend on drinks per visit?

clarifying_info.a: Kitchen: 4 staff at $10/hour when open; Bar: 1 staff at $5/hour; Waitresses: 3 staff at $5/hour
Food has a 20% gross margin (i.e., 80% COGS); Drinks have a 50% gross margin (i.e., 50% COGS)

clarifying_info.q: What are the operating hours and customer volumes?
clarifying_info.a: Sunday–Wednesday: 12pm–8pm (10 food/hr, 4 drinks/hr), 8pm–12am (4 food/hr, 15 drinks/hr); Thursday–Saturday: 12pm–8pm (15 food/hr, 5 drinks/hr), 8pm–2am (5 food/hr, 20 drinks/hr)

clarifying_info.q: Are there data on utilities, insurance, licenses, or startup costs?
clarifying_info.a: No specific data provided for utilities, legal, insurance, licenses, training, remodeling, equipment, or other startup costs

framework: Revenue analysis: estimate weekly food and drink revenue based on customer volumes, hours, and average spend
Cost analysis: calculate weekly COGS (food at 80%, drinks at 50%), weekly labor costs, and weekly lease costs
Weekly and annual profit: combine revenue and costs to derive net profit
Break-even and ROI: given $500K startup capital, calculate break-even period and 5-year return on investment
Investment comparison: frame profitability in context of alternative investments the father could make
Risks and missing costs: flag excluded costs (utilities, marketing) and external risks

questions.prompt: Calculate total weekly food and drink orders
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a table separating Sun–Wed vs Thu–Sat, day vs night, food vs drinks. Sun–Wed (4 days): daytime food = 10×8=80, daytime drinks = 4×8=32, night food = 4×4=16, night drinks = 15×4=60; daily food=96, daily drinks=92; weekly food=384, weekly drinks=368. Thu–Sat (3 days): daytime food = 15×8=120, daytime drinks = 5×8=40, night food = 5×6=30, night drinks = 20×6=120; daily food=150, daily drinks=160; weekly food=450, weekly drinks=480. Total weekly food orders = 384+450 = 834; total weekly drink orders = 368+480 = 848.

math.setup: Separate Sun–Wed (4 days, night ends 12am) from Thu–Sat (3 days, night ends 2am). Multiply customers/hour × hours for each segment.
math.answer: 834 weekly food orders; 848 weekly drink orders

questions.prompt: Calculate weekly revenue and weekly COGS
questions.guidance: Weekly food revenue = 834×$15 = $12,510; weekly drink revenue = 848×$20 = $16,960; total weekly revenue = $29,470. Food COGS = 80% of $12,510 = $10,008; drinks COGS = 50% of $16,960 = $8,480; total weekly COGS = $19,488.

math.setup: Revenue = orders × average spend. COGS = revenue × COGS percentage (food = 80%, drinks = 50%).
math.answer: Total weekly revenue = $29,470; total weekly COGS = $19,488

questions.guidance: Kitchen: 4 staff × $10/hr. Bar: 1 staff × $5/hr. Waitresses: 3 staff × $5/hr. Sun–Wed = 4 days × (12pm–12am) = 4×12 = 48 hours per role. Thu–Sat = 3 days × (12pm–2am) = 3×14 = 42 hours per role. Total hours = 48+42 = 90. Kitchen total = 4×$10×90 = $3,600; Bar total = 1×$5×90 = $450; Waitresses total = 3×$5×90 = $1,350. Total weekly labor = $5,400.

math.setup: Total hours per staff group = Sun–Wed hours + Thu–Sat hours. Multiply by number of staff and hourly rate.
steps: Sun–Wed hours per role = 4 days × 12 hours = 48
Thu–Sat hours per role = 3 days × 14 hours = 42

questions.guidance: Weekly lease = $10,000/4 weeks = $2,500. Weekly profit = $29,470 − $19,488 − $5,400 − $2,500 = $2,082. Assuming 50 operating weeks/year, annual profit = $2,082 × 50 = $104,100. Key takeaway: the business is not projected to lose money but cost assumptions may be incomplete.

math.setup: Weekly profit = weekly revenue − weekly COGS − weekly labor − weekly lease. Annual profit = weekly profit × 50 weeks.

questions.prompt: Given $500K startup capital, how long to break even? What is the 5-year ROI?
questions.guidance: Break-even = $500,000 / $104,100 ≈ 4.8 years. 5-year ROI = (($104,100 × 5) − $500,000) / $500,000 = ($520,500 − $500,000) / $500,000 = $20,500 / $500,000 ≈ 4.1%. The margin is small relative to the initial investment; the father could likely find another investment with faster payback and higher ROI.

math.setup: Break-even = startup costs / annual profit. 5-year ROI = (total 5-year profit − startup costs) / startup costs.
math.answer: Break-even ≈ 4.8 years; 5-year ROI ≈ 4.1% (less than 1% per year)

brainstorming.prompt: What additional revenue sources or cost-reduction strategies could improve the business plan?

categories.name: Additional revenue streams
ideas: Private event bookings and venue rental
Happy hour promotions to boost off-peak volume

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Purchase used kitchen equipment to reduce startup capital
Less significant interior redesign to lower renovation costs
Negotiate lease terms or find a less expensive location
Cross-train staff to reduce headcount during slow hours

categories.name: Pricing and margin improvement
ideas: Build brand and customer loyalty to justify higher prices over time
Shift menu mix toward higher-margin drinks
Introduce premium/specialty cocktails with higher margins

categories.name: Operational model
ideas: Focus operating hours on high-traffic Thu–Sat to reduce labor
Consider food vs. drinks focus based on margin analysis

recommendation: From a financial perspective the sports bar is projected to be profitable with an annual profit of approximately $104,100 on weekly revenue of ~$29,470, and a break-even period of ~4.8 years on $500K startup capital

However, the 5-year ROI is only ~4.1% (less than 1% per year), which is low compared to alternative investments; the client's father should benchmark this against other opportunities before committing capital
risks: Several costs have been excluded from the analysis (utilities, marketing and promotions, insurance, licenses) which will reduce actual profitability
Location is a critical success factor that has not been evaluated against competitors
External risks include a sudden rise in COGS (e.g., food shortage), an increase in minimum wages, or a decline in customer traffic after the initial opening period
next_steps: Incorporate utilities, marketing, and other excluded costs into the profitability model to produce a more accurate profit estimate
Investigate alternative investment opportunities available to the father to benchmark the sports bar's ROI
Explore ways to reduce startup capital (used equipment, scaled-down renovations) to shorten the break-even period
Assess location options and competitive landscape before committing to a site
